# Summary of Education in Nigeria
Education in Nigeria begins with six years of primary schooling starting around age five, culminating in a first school-leaving certificate. The subjects include Mathematics, English, religious knowledge, agricultural science, home economics, and indigenous languages, with private schools offering additional courses like Computer Science and French. The Universal Basic Education (UBE) system, established in 1999, guarantees free and compulsory nine-year formal education encompassing primary and junior secondary school, monitored by the Universal Basic Education Commission. Secondary education lasts six years, split evenly between junior and senior levels, with curricula covering a broad range of core and elective subjects. Admission into schools, particularly federal government colleges known as "unity schools," is merit-based via national examinations. Teacher qualifications vary by institution type, with federal schools generally having more qualified staff compared to many understaffed state schools.
Tertiary education in Nigeria comprises federal, state, and private universities, polytechnics, monotechnics, and colleges of education, overseen primarily by the Nigerian Universities Commission. Admission requirements include credit passes in the Senior Secondary Certificate Examination and performance in the Joint Admissions and Matriculation Board exam. Private education, including religious and international schools, is prominent but often expensive, offering smaller class sizes and improved facilities. Vocational education, managed by the National Board for Technical Education, includes certificates and apprenticeships, aimed at meeting labor market needs but challenged by outdated curricula and insufficient political support. Literacy rates remain low, particularly in northern regions, worsened by poverty, insecurity, and cultural factors. Efforts to improve female and rural education face obstacles including infrastructural deficits and militant activities. International education is growing, with Nigeria hosting over 129 international schools as of 2015. Overall, Nigeria’s education system grapples with inequality, funding challenges, and quality disparities across regions and school types.
